allusions.nt_words: ἔσται ἡ ῥίζα τοῦ Ἰεσσαί καί ὁ ἀνιστάμενος ἄρχειν ἐθνῶν ἐπί αὐτῷ ἔθνη ἐλπιοῦσι(ν)
allusions.ot_mt_form: וְהָיָה בַּיּוֹם הַהוּא שֹׁרֶשׁ יִשַׁי אֲשֶׁר עֹמֵד לְנֵס עַמִּים אֵלָיו גּוֹיִם יִדְרֹשׁוּ — 'And it shall be in that day, the root of Jesse who stands as a signal for peoples, to him nations shall inquire/seek'
allusions.ot_lxx_form: ἔσται ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ ἐκείνῃ ἡ ῥίζα τοῦ Ἰεσσαί καί ὁ ἀνιστάμενος ἄρχειν ἐθνῶν ἐπ' αὐτῷ ἔθνη ἐλπιοῦσιν — 'There shall be in that day the root of Jesse and the one rising to rule the nations; upon him nations shall hope'
allusions.textual_implication: Paul's citation follows the LXX with near-verbatim precision, omitting only the temporal phrase 'ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ ἐκείνῃ' ('in that day') found in the LXX but not required for his catena's rhetorical purpose. The LXX renders the Hebrew עֹמֵד לְנֵס ('standing as a signal/banner') with ὁ ἀνιστάμενος ἄρχειν ('the one rising to rule'), a rendering that dramatically heightens the messianic and eschatological profile of the figure—moving from a 'standard' or 'signal' to one who actively 'rises to rule,' evoking resurrection or enthronement. The MT's יִדְרֹשׁוּ ('shall seek/inquire') is rendered by the LXX as ἐλπιοῦσιν ('shall hope'), a theologically loaded translation that Paul preserves, aligning it perfectly with the theme of Gentile hope (ἐλπίς) that governs Romans 15:7–13.
allusions.textual_implication_plain: Paul is quoting directly from the Greek Old Testament (LXX), not the Hebrew, and the Greek translation had already shifted the meaning toward 'hope' and 'rising to rule' — ideas that fit Paul's message about Jesus perfectly. By omitting only the phrase 'in that day,' Paul tightens the citation to focus on Gentile hope, which is the climax of his argument.
allusions.scholarly_note: Beale and Carson (Commentary on the NT Use of the OT, p. 724) confirm that Paul follows the LXX essentially verbatim, with the omission of the temporal clause being the only notable divergence, and note that the LXX's ἐλπιοῦσιν is the hermeneutical linchpin of the entire catena in Rom 15:9–12, as Paul structures the whole unit around the motif of Gentile ἐλπίς.

summary_technical: Romans 15:12 constitutes a near-verbatim citation of LXX Isaiah 11:10, with Paul's only editorial intervention being the omission of the temporal clause ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ ἐκείνῃ; the LXX's distinctive renderings ὁ ἀνιστάμενος ἄρχειν and ἐλπιοῦσιν (for MT עֹמֵד לְנֵס and יִדְרֹשׁוּ respectively) are fully preserved, confirming Paul's dependence on a Greek Vorlage and demonstrating how the LXX's translation choices, possibly reflecting a messianic hermeneutic already operative in Hellenistic Judaism, undergird Paul's Christological and missiological argument. The citation functions as the climactic fourth member of a catena (Rom 15:9–12) in which ἐλπίς / ἐλπιοῦσιν serves as the rhetorical and theological fulcrum.
summary_plain: Paul quotes the Greek Old Testament almost word-for-word, and the Greek translation's key word 'hope' (instead of the Hebrew 'seek') is exactly what Paul needs to cap his argument that Gentiles find their hope in the Messiah descended from Jesse (David's father).

bibcrit_hypothesis.title: LXX's Messianic Reframing Enables Paul's Gentile-Hope Argument
bibcrit_hypothesis.reasoning: The LXX translator's choice to render יִדְרֹשׁוּ ('seek') as ἐλπιοῦσιν ('hope') and עֹמֵד לְנֵס ('standing as a signal') as ὁ ἀνιστάμενος ἄρχειν ('the one rising to rule') represents an interpretive tradition that had already moved Isaiah 11:10 in a royal-messianic and eschatological direction before Paul. Paul exploits this pre-existing LXX trajectory: the 'rising to rule' language resonates with resurrection/exaltation Christology, and ἐλπιοῦσιν becomes the thematic word that ties together the entire Jew-Gentile unity argument in Romans 15. This suggests Paul did not merely cite a convenient proof-text but selected a passage whose Greek form had already undergone the kind of messianic interpretation that his gospel required, reflecting what Hays calls 'metaleptic' engagement with a prophetic text whose fuller scriptural context (Isaianic new exodus and restoration) enriches Paul's vision of the eschatological community.
bibcrit_hypothesis.plain: The Greek translation of Isaiah had already reworded the original Hebrew in ways that pointed toward a coming king who would rise to rule the nations and inspire their 'hope' — and Paul recognized that this Greek wording fit his message about Jesus so well that he quoted it almost unchanged to cap his whole argument about Jews and Gentiles worshipping together.

_validation.confidence_note: The analysis accurately represents the textual relationship between Romans 15:12, LXX Isaiah 11:10, and the MT, with one specific citation reference that should be verified.
